AUD.stem: CPA firm provides IT system selection services to an audit client. Is independence impaired?
choices: No, if pre-approved by audit committee
No, if fee is less than 10% of total fees
AUD.explain: ET 1.295 prohibits services where CPA makes management decisions for audit clients. This creates self-review threat.

AUD.stem: An auditor discovered that the client's CFO owns 10% of the auditing firm. Which independence rule is violated?
choices: Direct financial interest - independence is impaired
Indirect financial interest - independence not impaired if immaterial
AUD.explain: AICPA Code 1.200.001 prohibits direct financial interests regardless of materiality. CFO ownership in audit firm creates impermissible direct interest.

ISC.stem: The board of Meridian Building Group approves a three-year IT strategy and a risk-appetite statement, then delegates system selection and project execution to the CIO's team. In IT governance terms, the board is performing which set of activities?
choices: Evaluate, direct, and monitor — governance activities
Plan, build, run, and monitor — management activities
Design and operation of application controls
Day-to-day IT service management under ITIL
ISC.explain: Governance (per COBIT) is the board-level Evaluate-Direct-Monitor loop: set direction, approve strategy and risk appetite, and monitor outcomes. (B) encodes the misconception that governance and management are the same layer — plan/build/run/monitor is what management (the CIO's team) does. (C) confuses strategic oversight with control design, an operational task. (D) confuses governance with ITIL service management, which is an operations framework, not board oversight.

ISC.stem: Northstar Services wants a single framework that links enterprise goals to IT goals and covers governance and management of enterprise IT end-to-end — not just cybersecurity or financial-reporting controls. Which framework best fits?
ISC.explain: COBIT is the end-to-end governance-and-management framework for enterprise IT, explicitly cascading enterprise goals to IT (alignment) goals. (A) encodes the misconception that any IT framework is interchangeable — NIST CSF is scoped to cybersecurity risk (Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover), not enterprise IT governance. (B) is entity-level internal control over reporting/operations/compliance, not IT-specific governance. (D) ITIL is IT service management (incident, change, service delivery), an operational subset.

ISC.stem: At a construction-services firm, the lead application developer also holds credentials that let her migrate her own code into the production payroll environment. No one else reviews the migrations. The PRIMARY control concern is:
choices: The developer may lack sufficient programming skill
Inadequate segregation of duties between development and production migration
The payroll application lacks input edit checks
The firm has not adopted an agile methodology
ISC.explain: Developers should not move their own code to production; an independent function (change control/operations or an automated pipeline with independent approval) should migrate tested, approved code. This SoD failure lets unauthorized or erroneous code reach production undetected. (A) encodes the misconception that this is a competence issue — it is an access/authority issue regardless of skill. (C) is an application-control issue unrelated to the migration risk described. (D) encodes the misconception that methodology choice is a control; agile teams still require independent release controls.

ISC.stem: Meridian Building Group receives more system-project requests than it can fund. Which body is BEST positioned to prioritize competing IT projects against business strategy and approve resource allocation?
ISC.explain: An IT steering committee — senior business and IT leadership — exists precisely to align the project portfolio with strategy, prioritize competing requests, and approve funding. (A) encodes the misconception that technical custodians set priorities; DBAs administer data platforms, they don't own portfolio decisions. (B) external auditors must remain independent and cannot make management decisions. (C) the help desk is an operational support function with no portfolio authority.

ISC.stem: Northstar Services outsources hosted job-cost processing to a cloud vendor. Which contract provision MOST directly preserves Northstar's ability to obtain assurance over the vendor's controls?
choices: A clause requiring the vendor to use agile development
A right-to-audit clause and required delivery of periodic SOC reports
ISC.explain: Assurance over an outsourced provider comes from audit rights and/or independent SOC reporting — the contract must secure one or both. (A) is commercial pricing protection, not assurance. (B) encodes the misconception that a development methodology provides control assurance; it does not. (C) is a convenience term that, if anything, weakens leverage over the vendor.

ISC.stem: Estimators at a builder began pasting confidential bid data into a free public generative-AI tool they adopted without IT approval. Governance had no AI policy. Which response BEST addresses the root governance failure rather than just the symptom?
choices: Block the specific AI website at the firewall and take no further action
Terminate the estimators who used the tool
Establish an acceptable-use policy for emerging technology, an approval path for new tools, and monitoring for unsanctioned (shadow IT) usage
Prohibit all use of AI tools permanently across the company
ISC.explain: The root failure is governance of emerging technology: no policy, no intake/approval process, no monitoring — so shadow IT filled the vacuum. A policy + approval path + monitoring addresses cause, enables safe adoption, and covers the next tool, not just this one. (A) encodes the symptom-fix misconception — blocking one URL leaves the governance gap (and hundreds of other tools) open. (B) punishes users without fixing the missing policy they never had. (D) encodes the over-control misconception — blanket bans drive usage further underground and forfeit legitimate value.

ISC.stem: A reviewer classifies a control described as 'all changes to the job-cost application must be tested and approved before release to production.' Under the standard ITGC domains, this control belongs to:
ISC.explain: Testing and approving modifications to an existing application before release is the change-management domain. (B) encodes the misconception that everything touching production is 'access' — access controls govern who can log in and what they can do, not how changes are authorized. (C) operations covers scheduling, backups, and incident handling of running systems. (D) program development governs building NEW systems; changing an existing one is change management.

ISC.stem: A payroll clerk signs in with a password and then must approve a push notification on a registered phone. A second system requires a password plus answers to security questions. Which statement is correct?
choices: Only the first system uses multifactor authentication; a password plus security questions is two instances of one factor (something you know)
Neither system uses multifactor authentication because biometrics are required for MFA
The second system is stronger because security questions cannot be phished
ISC.explain: MFA requires factors from DIFFERENT categories: something you know, something you have, something you are. Password (know) + registered phone (have) = two factors. Password + security questions = know + know = single-factor, twice. (A) encodes the misconception that two challenges equal two factors. (C) encodes the misconception that biometrics are mandatory — any two distinct categories qualify. (D) is backwards; security-question answers are notoriously guessable and phishable.

ISC.stem: A newly hired AP clerk at Meridian Building Group was granted the same access profile as her supervisor 'to save setup time,' including vendor-master maintenance and payment release. The BEST characterization of the control failure is:
choices: A violation of the least-privilege principle in user provisioning, creating a segregation-of-duties conflict
A failure of physical access controls
An acceptable practice as long as her password is strong
ISC.explain: Provisioning should grant only the access a role requires (least privilege); giving a clerk vendor-master AND payment-release rights combines incompatible duties (can create a vendor and pay it). (B) confuses logical access with physical access. (C) encodes the misconception that authentication strength compensates for excessive authorization — a strong password just securely authenticates an over-privileged user. (D) mislabels the failure: provisioning is a preventive control; the failure is preventive, though a detective access review could catch it later.

ISC.stem: A project manager left Northstar Services in March; in June his network account was still active and had been used remotely. Which control, operating properly, would have DETECTED this condition?
choices: A periodic user-access review reconciling active accounts to current HR records
ISC.explain: A periodic access review compares active accounts against the current employee roster and flags terminated users — a detective control for deprovisioning failures. (A) firewalls filter network traffic; a valid account passes right through. (B) is an application input control, irrelevant to account lifecycle. (D) encryption protects data confidentiality but does nothing about a live authorized credential.

ISC.stem: A timekeeping application rejects any weekly timesheet entry over 100 hours for one employee. This input control is BEST described as a:
choices: Validity check against a master file
Check digit on the employee number
ISC.explain: A limit/reasonableness check tests whether a numeric value falls within a plausible range — 100 hours/week is the ceiling here. (A) encodes the misconception that all edits are lookups; a validity check compares input to authorized values (e.g., a real employee ID), not to a numeric bound. (B) completeness ensures all records/fields are present, not that values are reasonable. (D) a check digit detects transcription errors in identification numbers, not out-of-range quantities.

ISC.stem: Classify these three controls: (1) a firewall blocking unauthorized inbound traffic; (2) weekly review of failed-login logs; (3) restoring a corrupted file from last night's backup.
ISC.explain: Preventive controls stop errors/attacks before they occur (firewall). Detective controls identify events after they occur (log review). Corrective controls fix the damage (restoring from backup). (A) swaps the firewall and log review — a log review can only find what already happened, it prevents nothing. (C) encodes the misconception that fixing something you found makes the review corrective; the review detects, the restore corrects. (D) reverses the whole taxonomy.

ISC.stem: During a production outage at 2 a.m., an engineer applied an emergency code fix directly to the live job-cost system without prior approval. Which control package makes emergency changes acceptable rather than a deficiency?
choices: Emergency changes are never acceptable; the system must stay down until the full change process completes
Automatic logging of the change, documented after-the-fact approval within a defined window, and independent post-implementation review of the fix
Requiring the engineer to email the CIO the next week if he remembers
Granting all senior engineers permanent production access so approvals are unnecessary
ISC.explain: Standard practice permits emergency changes when compensating controls exist: the change is logged automatically, formally approved retroactively within a defined period, and independently reviewed afterward. (A) encodes the rigidity misconception — availability objectives justify an emergency path, provided it is controlled. (C) is an uncontrolled, unenforced notification, not a control. (D) encodes the misconception that removing the control removes the risk; standing production access for developers is itself a classic ITGC deficiency.

ISC.stem: Ransomware encrypts a contractor's estimating database, and no one can retrieve project data until systems are restored. Which element of the CIA triad is PRIMARILY compromised?
ISC.explain: Ransomware's primary effect is denying access to data and systems — an availability loss. (A) encodes the misconception that encryption events are confidentiality events; unless data was also exfiltrated, nothing was disclosed. (B) authorization is an access-control concept, not a CIA element. (D) non-repudiation concerns proving who performed an action; it is not one of the CIA triad elements and is not the issue here.

ISC.stem: Before a new billing system goes live, who should perform user acceptance testing (UAT), and when?
choices: The business users who will operate the system, after system/integration testing and before implementation
The developers who wrote the code, immediately after unit testing
The external auditor, after the system is in production
The vendor's sales team, during requirements definition
ISC.explain: UAT is the business users' confirmation that the system meets requirements in realistic scenarios; it follows system and integration testing and gates go-live. (B) encodes the misconception that developers can accept their own work — that is self-review; developers do unit testing, not acceptance. (C) auditors may review the process but do not perform UAT, and after go-live is too late to 'accept.' (D) sales has no acceptance role, and testing cannot precede a built system.

ISC.stem: Meridian Building Group is replacing its payroll system. An error at go-live would mean employees are paid incorrectly. Management wants the LOWEST-risk conversion approach and accepts higher cost. Which strategy fits?
choices: Direct (big-bang) cutover on the first payday of the year
Parallel operation — run old and new systems together and reconcile results for several pay cycles
Phased conversion by module with no overlap of systems
Pilot conversion at one job site with immediate shutdown of the old system everywhere
ISC.explain: Parallel operation is the classic lowest-risk (and most expensive) strategy: both systems process the same payrolls and outputs are reconciled, so the old system is a live fallback. (A) direct cutover is the cheapest and riskiest — no fallback if the new system miscalculates pay. (C) phased limits scope but each phase is still a cutover with no side-by-side verification. (D) encodes a contradiction: a true pilot keeps the old system running for non-pilot sites; shutting it down everywhere destroys the safety the pilot was meant to provide.

ISC.stem: During migration of 48,000 vendor records to a new ERP, which control MOST directly verifies that the migration was complete and accurate?
choices: Requiring MFA for the migration team
Encrypting the extract files in transit
Reconciling record counts and control totals (e.g., total open AP balance) between source and target, plus sample field-level comparisons
Having the project sponsor sign the project charter
ISC.explain: Completeness and accuracy of converted data are verified by reconciliation: record counts, hash/control totals on key balances, and field-level sampling between source and target. (A) MFA protects who performs the migration, not whether the data arrived intact. (B) encryption protects confidentiality in transit but a complete, accurate ciphertext of a botched extract is still botched. (D) a charter authorizes the project; it verifies nothing about data fidelity.

ISC.stem: A firm must build a compliance-reporting system whose requirements are fixed by regulation, fully specifiable up front, and unlikely to change. Documentation and formal sign-offs at each stage are required by the regulator. Which methodology is the BEST fit?
choices: Scrum with two-week sprints and evolving requirements
Kanban with continuous deployment to production
No formal methodology — ad hoc development
Waterfall, with sequential phases and stage-gate sign-offs
ISC.explain: Waterfall suits stable, fully specifiable requirements with mandated documentation and sequential approvals — exactly this scenario. (A) encodes the 'agile is always better' misconception; agile's strength is adapting to CHANGING requirements, which is not the situation, and sprint-based evolution complicates fixed regulatory sign-offs. (B) continuous deployment conflicts with stage-gate regulatory approval. (D→C) ad hoc development is a control failure, not a methodology.

ISC.stem: A new estimating system went live. Which combination BEST reflects proper implementation-stage segregation and follow-up?
choices: Developers migrate their own code to production; the project manager performs the post-implementation review

An independent migration function (or controlled automated pipeline) moves approved code; business owner formally accepts; a post-implementation review — independent of the project team — evaluates whether objectives and benefits were achieved
Operations migrates the code, and no post-implementation review is needed if UAT passed
The steering committee migrates the code personally to ensure tone at the top
ISC.explain: Correct design: migration to production by a party independent of development (librarian function or controlled CI/CD with independent approval), formal business acceptance, and an independent post-implementation review of outcomes vs. business case. (A) fails twice — developer self-migration breaks SoD, and the PM reviewing his own project breaks review independence. (C) encodes the misconception that UAT passing ends accountability; PIR evaluates realized benefits and residual issues UAT cannot. (D) is an absurd role confusion — governance bodies oversee, they don't execute operational tasks.

ISC.stem: A developer wants to test a payroll code fix using the live production database 'because the data is realistic.' The BEST response is:
choices: Allow it, since realistic data produces the best tests
Allow it if the developer promises to be careful
Require testing in a separate environment using masked or sanitized copies of production data
Cancel all testing and deploy directly
ISC.explain: Testing belongs in a non-production environment; if production-like data is needed, it should be masked/sanitized to protect confidential payroll information. This preserves both production integrity and data privacy. (A) encodes the realism-over-control misconception — realistic data can be achieved with masked copies without risking live records and exposing PII. (B) a promise is not a control. (D) skipping testing entirely maximizes the very risk testing exists to reduce.

ISC.stem: A clerk tries to enter a sales order for customer number 9930, which does not exist in the customer table, and the database rejects the insert. Which constraint produced the rejection?
choices: Referential integrity enforced through a foreign key
Entity integrity on the order table's primary key
ISC.explain: The order row's customer number is a foreign key that must match an existing primary key in the customer table — referential integrity blocks orphan records. (B) field length restricts characters, not relationships. (C) encodes primary/foreign key confusion: entity integrity requires the ORDER's own key to be unique and non-null; it says nothing about the customer reference. (D) UI conventions are not database constraints.

ISC.stem: Month-end analytical queries run directly against Northstar's live order-entry database are slowing customer transactions to a crawl. The standard architectural remedy is to:
choices: Delete historical data so queries run faster
Extract data to a separate data warehouse structured for analysis, and point reporting there
Ask analysts to run queries only at night, permanently
Denormalize the live transactional database into star schemas
ISC.explain: OLTP systems are optimized for many small transactions; analytical workloads belong in a separate warehouse (dimensional/star structures) fed by ETL, isolating reporting load from operations. (A) destroys the historical data analysis needs and creates retention problems. (C) is a scheduling workaround, not an architecture — it caps analysis capacity and fails as data grows. (D) encodes the misconception that you restructure the LIVE system; denormalizing the transactional database degrades transaction processing and update integrity.

ISC.stem: During the nightly ETL load from the job-cost system to the data warehouse, which control set MOST directly addresses the risk that records are dropped or altered in transformation?
choices: Batch control totals and record counts reconciled at each stage, with an exception/error log that is reviewed and resolved
A strong password on the warehouse administrator account
Purchasing more storage for the warehouse
Restricting the warehouse to read-only for all users
ISC.explain: Completeness/accuracy through a pipeline is controlled with stage-to-stage reconciliation of counts and control totals plus managed exception handling. (B) access control protects against unauthorized change, not transformation errors in the pipeline itself. (C) capacity is an availability concern, irrelevant to dropped records. (D) read-only access for consumers protects data after it lands but does nothing about what the ETL job dropped on the way in.

ISC.stem: A regional manager requests access to the full employee-compensation dataset. Under a data-governance model, who has the AUTHORITY to approve or deny the request?
choices: The database administrator, as the person who technically grants access
Any user who already has access to the data
The data owner accountable for the compensation data (e.g., the HR executive)
The data steward, because stewards outrank owners
ISC.explain: Data owners are the accountable business executives who decide who may access their data and under what conditions; custodians then implement the decision. (A) encodes the classic owner/custodian confusion — the DBA is a custodian who EXECUTES approved grants but does not approve them. (B) access does not confer authority to share. (D) inverts the hierarchy: stewards manage data quality and definitions day-to-day on behalf of owners; they don't outrank them.

ISC.stem: A firm's policy requires payroll records to be kept seven years and then securely destroyed with documented certificates of destruction. These requirements govern which stages of the data life cycle?
ISC.explain: Retention periods and defensible, documented destruction are the end-of-life stages of the data life cycle. (A) creation/capture governs how data enters the environment. (C) analysis is a usage stage — retention rules are not about how data is analyzed. (D) ingestion/transformation are pipeline stages that occur while data is active, not how long it is kept or how it is disposed of.

ISC.stem: Northstar discovers the same customer exists in its billing master file five times with slightly different name spellings, causing understated concentration reports. This is PRIMARILY a failure of which data-quality dimension, and what is the standard remedy?
choices: Timeliness; refresh the file more often
Validity; the records violate field formats
Uniqueness; deduplicate via matching rules and enforce a single golden record (master data management)
ISC.explain: Duplicate representations of one real-world entity violate uniqueness; the remedy is matching/merge rules and master data management to maintain one authoritative record. (A) encodes the misconception that stale data causes duplicates — refresh frequency won't merge them. (B) is the opposite problem; nothing is missing, there is too much. (C) each duplicate may be perfectly valid in format — validity checks won't catch semantically duplicate records.

ISC.stem: A CFO proposes dumping all raw operational, IoT-sensor, and document data into a low-cost central repository with schema applied only when data is read, to enable future analytics. Which statement about this architecture and its PRIMARY governance risk is most accurate?
choices: It is a data warehouse, and the primary risk is that schema-on-write is too flexible
It is a data lake (schema-on-read); without cataloging, ownership, and quality controls it degrades into an ungoverned 'data swamp' of unusable, potentially sensitive data
It is an OLTP system, and the primary risk is transaction locking
It is a blockchain, and the primary risk is proof-of-work energy cost
ISC.explain: Storing raw, multi-format data with schema-on-read defines a data lake; its characteristic governance failure is the data swamp — no catalog, no owners, unknown quality, and sensitive data with no classification or access rules. (A) reverses the concepts: warehouses use schema-on-WRITE and curated structures, and rigidity (not flexibility) is their trade-off. (C) an OLTP system is the opposite: highly structured, transaction-optimized. (D) is a category error — nothing described involves distributed ledgers.
refs: Data lake vs. warehouse; data swamp risk

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: Meridian Building Group outsources payroll processing to a service organization. Meridian's financial statement auditor wants assurance over the service organization's controls that affect Meridian's payroll balances. Which report is designed for this need?
choices: A SOC 2 report on security and availability
ISC.explain: SOC 1 reports address controls at a service organization relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting — exactly what a user auditor needs for outsourced payroll. (B) encodes the misconception that SOC 2 is the universal report; it addresses trust services criteria (security, availability, etc.) for operational/compliance needs, not ICFR assertions. (C) SOC 3 is a marketing-oriented summary lacking the detail user auditors need. (D) PCI DSS is card-data compliance, unrelated to payroll ICFR.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A user auditor plans to rely on a service organization's controls over transaction processing for the ENTIRE year under audit. Which SOC report provides the needed evidence?
choices: A Type 1 report as of the balance-sheet date
A Type 1 report as of the first day of the year
Either type, because they provide identical assurance
A Type 2 report covering the period, because it tests operating effectiveness over time
ISC.explain: Type 2 reports opine on design AND operating effectiveness over a specified period, which is what control reliance for a period requires. (A) and (B) encode the point-in-time misconception: a Type 1 addresses design/implementation at a single date only — it says nothing about whether controls OPERATED all year. (C) is false; the assurance levels differ fundamentally — operating effectiveness is only tested in a Type 2.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A cloud provider wants a report on its security controls that it can post publicly on its website for prospective customers. Which report is appropriate?
choices: SOC 1 Type 2, because it is the most detailed
ISC.explain: SOC 3 is the general-use trust-services report designed for unrestricted distribution (no detailed test results). (A) SOC 1 addresses ICFR-relevant controls and is restricted-use — wrong subject and wrong audience. (C) encodes the distribution misconception: SOC 2 reports are restricted-use (specified parties who understand the system); they are not for public posting. (D) an internal memo is not independent assurance.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A payroll service organization uses a third-party cloud data center. The payroll company's SOC 1 report describes the data center's controls as excluded, listing instead the controls the payroll company expects the data center to have. This treatment is called:
choices: A scope limitation requiring a disclaimer of opinion
The carve-out method, identifying complementary subservice organization controls
A qualified opinion on the data center
ISC.explain: Carve-out excludes the subservice organization's controls from the description and tests, while identifying the complementary subservice organization controls (CSOCs) assumed to be in place. (A) is the opposite: inclusive method brings the subservice org's controls INTO the description and testing. (B) encodes the misconception that carve-out is an audit problem — it is a permitted presentation method, not a scope limitation. (D) no opinion is being expressed on the data center at all under carve-out.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A user entity relies on a payroll service organization whose SOC 1 Type 2 report carves out its cloud-hosting subservice organization. What must the user entity (and its auditor) do about the hosting risk?
choices: Nothing — the payroll SOC 1 opinion automatically covers the carved-out data center
Obtain assurance over the subservice organization separately (e.g., its own SOC report) or otherwise evaluate whether the identified complementary subservice organization controls are in place
Refuse to rely on any part of the payroll SOC 1 report
Require the payroll company to insource its hosting before year-end
ISC.explain: Under carve-out, the service auditor's opinion does NOT cover the subservice organization; users must bridge the gap — typically by obtaining the subservice org's own SOC report or performing other procedures over the CSOCs. (A) encodes the coverage misconception that is the whole point of carve-out — coverage stops at the carve-out line. (C) overcorrects: the report remains valid evidence for the controls it does cover. (D) is an unrealistic business demand, not an assurance procedure.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A service organization's SOC 1 report lists as a complementary user-entity control (CUEC): 'User entities are responsible for restricting who can submit payroll changes.' A user entity never restricted submission access, and a fraudulent pay-rate change was processed. Which statement is correct?
choices: The service organization's controls failed, because the fraud flowed through its system
The service auditor should have caught the user's weakness during the SOC examination
A CUEC breakdown is impossible when the SOC opinion is unqualified
The control failure is the user entity's: the SOC report's control objectives are achieved only if user entities implement the stated CUECs
ISC.explain: CUECs are controls the service organization ASSUMES user entities will operate; the SOC opinion is conditioned on them. Failing to implement a CUEC is a user-entity control failure, not a service-organization failure. (A) encodes the misconception that the processor owns all risk in its pipeline — it explicitly disclaimed this piece via the CUEC. (B) service auditors examine the service organization; they do not audit each user's controls. (C) an unqualified SOC opinion says nothing about whether any particular user actually implemented the CUECs.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: Which element appears in a SOC 1 Type 2 report but NOT in a SOC 1 Type 1 report?
choices: Management's description of the service organization's system
The service auditor's description of tests of controls and results for the period
ISC.explain: Both types contain the system description, management's assertion, and an opinion; only a Type 2 adds the detailed tests of operating effectiveness and their results over the period. (A), (B), and (D) all encode the misconception that Type 1 reports are missing basic elements — Type 1 has all three; what it lacks is testing of operating effectiveness over time.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A user auditor receives a SOC 1 Type 2 report with a qualified opinion: controls over one objective — automated interest calculations — did not operate effectively. The user auditor's BEST response is to:
choices: Discard the entire report and treat the service organization as unaudited
Assess whether the qualified area is relevant to the user's financial statements and, if so, respond with substantive procedures or testing of compensating controls over interest calculations
Rely on the report in full, since most objectives were met
Require the client to change service organizations before issuing the audit opinion
ISC.explain: A qualification is objective-specific: the auditor maps the failed objective to relevant assertions and designs a response (substantive testing, user-entity compensating controls) for that area, while still relying on unaffected areas. (A) over-rejects — the unqualified portions remain valid evidence. (C) under-responds by ignoring a directly relevant failure. (D) confuses an evidence problem with a business decision the auditor cannot impose.
refs: Using SOC reports with modified opinions

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: Bluewater SaaS, a project-management platform, keeps losing enterprise deals because prospects' vendor-risk teams demand independent evidence about its security and availability controls. Which engagement should Bluewater pursue?
choices: A SOC 2 Type 2 examination on security and availability
An agreed-upon procedures report on its marketing claims
ISC.explain: Vendor-risk diligence about security/availability maps to SOC 2 on the relevant trust services categories, and Type 2 provides operating-effectiveness evidence buyers expect. (B) encodes SOC 1/SOC 2 confusion — SOC 1 targets user ICFR, not security posture, and Type 1 lacks period coverage. (C) a financial statement audit says nothing about platform controls. (D) AUP procedures don't provide the recognized, criteria-based assurance vendor-risk teams request.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A user entity's fiscal year ends December 31. Its service organization's SOC 1 Type 2 report covers October 1 of the prior year through September 30. How should the user auditor address October–December?
choices: Ignore the gap; three months is automatically immaterial
Obtain a bridge (gap) letter from the service organization about changes since September 30, evaluate any changes, and perform additional procedures as needed for the stub period
Insist the service auditor reissue the same report dated December 31
Treat the entire year as unaudited and disclaim an opinion
ISC.explain: The standard response to a coverage gap is a bridge letter (management's statement of whether controls changed after the period), evaluation of any identified changes, and supplemental procedures (inquiry, testing) proportionate to the gap and risk. (A) encodes the misconception that short gaps need no consideration — the auditor must assess, not assume. (C) a report cannot simply be redated; it covers the period tested. (D) is a massive overreaction — a manageable evidence gap does not force a disclaimer.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A company scoping its first SOC 2 asks which trust services category CANNOT be excluded. The correct answer is:
choices: Availability, because customers care about uptime most
Security, because the common criteria are required in every SOC 2 examination
Processing integrity, because SOC 2 originated from transaction processing
ISC.explain: Security (the common criteria) is mandatory in every SOC 2; the other four categories — availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy — are added based on commitments and user needs. (A) encodes the misconception that privacy is compulsory; it is optional unless personal-information commitments make it relevant. (B) availability is common but elective. (D) processing integrity is likewise elective; the historical origin claim is also wrong.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A billing platform's nightly batch job silently dropped 2% of usage records last quarter, so invoices were incomplete — though the system was online 99.99% of the time. Which trust services category is implicated?
choices: Availability, because a batch job failed
Processing integrity, because processing was not complete and accurate
Privacy, because customer invoices were involved
Confidentiality, because usage data was lost
ISC.explain: Processing integrity addresses whether processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized — dropped records violate completeness/accuracy even with perfect uptime. (A) encodes the misconception that any batch failure is availability; the SYSTEM was available — its output was wrong. (C) privacy concerns collection/use/disclosure of PERSONAL information, not billing accuracy. (D) confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure; nothing was disclosed — data was dropped.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A SOC 2 candidate handles two data sets: (1) customers' proprietary pricing models covered by NDAs, and (2) personal information of customers' employees collected for benefits administration. How do the trust services categories map?
choices: Pricing models → confidentiality; employees' personal information → privacy
Both → privacy, because both are sensitive
Both → confidentiality, because privacy applies only to healthcare entities
Pricing models → privacy; personal information → confidentiality
ISC.explain: Confidentiality covers information designated as confidential (business data, NDAs); privacy applies specifically to PERSONAL information and the commitments around its collection, use, retention, disclosure, and disposal. (B) encodes the 'sensitive = privacy' misconception — privacy is scoped to personal information, not all sensitive data. (C) invents a healthcare limitation that doesn't exist. (D) reverses the two categories.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A SaaS provider's customer contracts promise 99.9% uptime and financially credit customers for missed service levels. Its current SOC 2 covers security only. What should scoping recommend?
choices: Keep security only; uptime is a business matter outside SOC 2
Replace security with availability, since only one category is allowed
Add processing integrity, because uptime is about processing
Add the availability category, because the company makes explicit availability commitments to customers
ISC.explain: Categories are added when the entity makes commitments or has system requirements in that domain — a contractual uptime SLA is the textbook trigger for including availability. (A) encodes the misconception that contractual commitments are out of scope; commitments are exactly what SOC 2 examines. (B) is structurally wrong — security is always required and multiple categories can be combined. (C) misclassifies uptime: availability is about accessibility for operation, processing integrity about correctness of processing.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: Under the trust services criteria, processing integrity means system processing is:
choices: Complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized
ISC.explain: The definition is the five attributes: complete, valid, accurate, timely, authorized. (B) mixes security and availability mechanisms — controls that may SUPPORT integrity but are not its definition. (C) lists performance/economic qualities outside assurance criteria entirely. (D) lists specific security/operations controls, again mechanisms rather than the defined attributes.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: During SOC 2 readiness, a controller worries the company must implement every 'point of focus' listed under each common criterion. The service auditor's BEST clarification is:
choices: Correct — every point of focus is a required control that must exist
Points of focus apply only to privacy engagements
Points of focus replace the criteria when they conflict
Points of focus are illustrative considerations that help evaluate whether a criterion is met; the entity need not address each one if the criterion is otherwise satisfied
ISC.explain: Points of focus are guidance — characteristics that MAY be relevant when evaluating a criterion. The opinion is on the criteria, not on point-by-point compliance. (A) encodes the checklist misconception that turns guidance into requirements. (B) they exist across the criteria, not just privacy. (C) inverts the hierarchy — criteria always govern; points of focus never override them.

ISC.blueprintArea: Considerations for System and Organization Controls (SOC) Engagements
ISC.stem: A service organization encrypts customer data files at rest and tightly manages the encryption keys. In a SOC 2 covering security, availability, and confidentiality, how does this ONE control map to the criteria?
choices: It maps only to availability, because encrypted data is always recoverable
It cannot be used for more than one criterion; a duplicate control must be built for each category
It can support multiple criteria simultaneously — e.g., logical access/data protection under the security common criteria and protection of confidential information under confidentiality
It maps to processing integrity, because encryption guarantees accurate processing
ISC.explain: Controls map many-to-many against criteria: encryption at rest with key management is classic evidence for security common criteria (protection of data, logical access) AND for confidentiality commitments. (A) is backwards — encryption does nothing for availability, and lost keys actually create an availability risk. (B) encodes the one-control-one-criterion misconception; a single well-designed control routinely serves several criteria. (D) overstates encryption: it protects data from disclosure/alteration in storage but cannot make processing logic accurate.

ISC.stem: Northstar's AP clerk receives an urgent email appearing to come from the CFO, instructing an immediate $85,000 wire to a 'new subcontractor' and demanding secrecy. Which control MOST directly defeats this attack?
choices: Out-of-band verification — confirming any payment-instruction change with the requester by a known phone number before release
Stronger password complexity requirements for the clerk
Full-disk encryption on the clerk's laptop
Increasing the email server's storage quota
ISC.explain: This is business email compromise, a social-engineering attack on the payment process; the defeating control is procedural — independent, out-of-band confirmation of payment instructions using known contact details. (B) encodes the misconception that authentication controls stop social engineering; no password was attacked. (C) disk encryption protects a stolen device, irrelevant here. (D) is a red-herring capacity item with no control value.

ISC.stem: An analyst confirms ransomware is actively spreading from one workstation across the network. The IMMEDIATE next step in the incident-response life cycle is:
choices: Contain the incident — isolate the infected machine and affected segments from the network
Restore all systems from backup while the malware is still active
ISC.explain: After detection/analysis confirms an active incident, containment comes next — stop the spread by isolating affected systems. (A) lessons learned is the FINAL phase. (C) paying is a business/legal decision, never the reflex 'next step,' and doesn't stop active spread. (D) encodes a sequencing error — recovery before eradication just re-infects restored systems.

ISC.stem: A CISO argues that because the company bought a 'next-generation firewall,' additional controls like endpoint protection, MFA, and log monitoring are redundant spending. The BEST rebuttal is grounded in which principle?
choices: Zero-day tolerance — modern firewalls cannot be breached
Defense in depth — layered, overlapping controls so that failure or bypass of any single control does not expose the whole environment
Security through obscurity — hiding the network design is sufficient
Single point of accountability — one control makes audits simpler
ISC.explain: Defense in depth assumes any single control can fail or be bypassed (phishing sails past a firewall entirely), so protection is layered: network, endpoint, identity, monitoring. (A) is a false premise — every control has bypasses and vulnerabilities. (C) obscurity is explicitly rejected as a primary defense. (D) encodes the misconception that audit convenience is a security design principle; concentrating everything in one control creates a single point of failure.

ISC.stem: A firm's security model grants full internal-network access to any device that connects from inside the office ('trusted zone'). A consultant recommends zero trust. Which change BEST reflects the zero-trust model?
choices: A taller perimeter: stronger firewall rules at the office boundary, with the interior unchanged
Trusting all traffic that originates from company-owned devices
Removing authentication for internal apps to reduce friction
Authenticate and authorize every access request continuously — per user, per device, per resource — regardless of network location
ISC.explain: Zero trust replaces location-based trust ('inside = safe') with continuous verification of identity, device posture, and authorization for each resource request. (A) encodes the perimeter misconception zero trust exists to fix — a harder shell with a soft interior. (B) device ownership is not trust; compromised corporate devices are a primary attack path. (C) is the opposite of the model — zero trust adds verification, it never removes authentication.

ISC.stem: Order these incident-response activities per the standard life cycle: (1) remove the malware and close the exploited vulnerability; (2) restore systems to normal operation; (3) develop the IR plan and train the team; (4) triage alerts to confirm an incident; (5) isolate affected systems.
ISC.explain: The life cycle runs Preparation (3) → Detection & Analysis (4) → Containment (5) → Eradication (1) → Recovery (2) → Lessons Learned. (B) puts preparation after detection — preparation by definition precedes incidents — and restores before eradicating, which re-infects clean systems. (C) contains before confirming an incident exists, disrupting operations on unverified alerts. (D) also isolates before any analysis and places preparation mid-incident.

ISC.stem: The audit committee asks the difference between the quarterly 'vulnerability scans' IT runs and the annual 'penetration test' by an outside firm. The BEST distinction is:
choices: Scans automatically identify and rank known weaknesses; a penetration test has skilled humans actively attempt to EXPLOIT weaknesses and chain them to demonstrate real-world impact
They are identical; the pen test just costs more
Scans are performed only by attackers; pen tests only by regulators
A pen test is passive observation, while scanning involves active exploitation
ISC.explain: Vulnerability scanning is automated identification/prioritization of known flaws; penetration testing is authorized, human-driven exploitation that proves what an attacker could actually achieve (chained attacks, privilege escalation). (B) encodes the interchangeability misconception — depth and evidence differ fundamentally. (C) both are legitimate internal/third-party practices; neither belongs to attackers or regulators. (D) reverses the two definitions.

ISC.stem: A firm encrypts backups with a strong algorithm but stores the encryption keys in the same cloud folder as the encrypted backup files, readable by all IT staff. The PRIMARY problem is:
choices: The algorithm should be replaced with a proprietary secret algorithm
Encrypting backups is unnecessary in the first place
Key management failure — co-locating keys with ciphertext and over-broad key access defeats the encryption's protection
Backups should never be stored in the cloud
ISC.explain: Encryption is only as strong as its key management: anyone who obtains the folder gets both ciphertext and key, and every IT employee can decrypt. Keys must be stored separately (KMS/HSM) with restricted, logged access. (A) encodes security-through-obscurity — proprietary secret algorithms are weaker than vetted public ones. (B) abandons a needed control instead of fixing its implementation. (D) mislocates the issue; cloud storage is fine with proper key separation.

ISC.stem: During bid week, a builder's customer portal is knocked offline by massive automated traffic from thousands of compromised devices worldwide. Which attack is this, and which control set MOST directly mitigates it?
choices: SQL injection; fix with parameterized queries
A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack; mitigate with traffic-scrubbing/CDN services, rate limiting, and redundant capacity
A brute-force password attack; mitigate with account lockouts
An insider threat; mitigate with segregation of duties
ISC.explain: Coordinated flood traffic from a botnet aimed at exhausting availability is a DDoS; mitigation is absorbing/filtering volume — scrubbing services, CDNs, rate limiting, redundancy. (A) encodes the 'all web attacks are injection' misconception; injection manipulates queries, it doesn't flood capacity, and parameterized queries do nothing against volume. (C) brute force targets credentials, and lockouts would not reduce network-level flooding. (D) nothing indicates an insider; SoD is a process control irrelevant to traffic floods.

ISC.stem: An intrusion detection system (IDS) that alerts the security team to suspicious traffic — but does not block it — is BEST classified as what type of control?
ISC.explain: An IDS monitors and ALERTS — identifying events as or after they occur — the definition of a detective control. (B) encodes IDS/IPS confusion: an intrusion PREVENTION system blocks traffic inline and is preventive; detection-only is not. (A) corrective controls remediate damage (e.g., restore from backup). (C) compensating controls substitute for a missing primary control; that's a role, not what an IDS inherently is.

ISC.stem: Attackers extracted a service company's entire customer table by typing crafted text into the login form's username field, causing the database to execute the text as part of a query. Which vulnerability was exploited, and what is the PRIMARY fix?
choices: SQL injection; fix with input validation and parameterized queries/prepared statements (with a web application firewall as an additional layer)
Cross-site scripting; fix by encrypting the database
A DDoS attack; fix with more bandwidth
Weak passwords; fix with a longer password policy
ISC.explain: User input concatenated into a query and executed by the database is SQL injection; the root-cause fix is parameterized queries/prepared statements plus input validation, with a WAF as defense in depth. (B) misidentifies the attack — XSS executes script in a victim's BROWSER, not queries in the database — and encryption at rest doesn't stop a query the app itself executes. (C) nothing here concerns traffic volume. (D) encodes the misconception that login-page attacks are always credential attacks; no password was guessed — the form field was a code path.

ISC.stem: What is the key distinction between a business continuity plan (BCP) and a disaster recovery plan (DRP)?
choices: BCP addresses continuing critical BUSINESS operations during disruption; DRP is the narrower IT-focused plan for restoring systems, applications, and data
BCP is for natural disasters only; DRP is for cyberattacks only
They are the same document with different covers
DRP covers the whole business; BCP covers only IT
ISC.explain: BCP is the enterprise-wide plan for keeping critical business functions running (people, facilities, processes, communications); DRP is its IT component — restoring technology. (B) encodes a cause-based misconception; both plans are cause-agnostic. (C) understates real scope differences that drive different owners, testing, and content. (D) reverses the two scopes.

ISC.stem: A firm backs up its estimating database once nightly at 11:00 p.m. Management has declared a recovery point objective (RPO) of 4 hours for this system. A disk failure at 3:00 p.m. would lose all data entered since the prior 11:00 p.m. backup. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The RPO is met because backups run every day without fail
The failure is a recovery time objective (RTO) problem, not an RPO problem
The 4-hour RPO cannot be met — up to 16 hours of data would be lost — so the firm needs more frequent backups or continuous replication
The RPO should be redefined as 24 hours so the current backups comply
ISC.explain: RPO is maximum tolerable DATA loss measured in time. Nightly backups mean a worst-case loss approaching 24 hours (16 hours in this scenario: 11 p.m. to 3 p.m.), far beyond the 4-hour RPO; meeting it requires intra-day backups or replication. (A) encodes the reliability misconception — consistent daily backups still leave a 24-hour exposure window. (B) confuses the two objectives: RTO is downtime duration; lost transactions are RPO. (D) reverses the logic — objectives are set by business impact (the BIA), then capabilities are built to meet them, not defined down to match current practice.

ISC.stem: Before selecting recovery strategies, a continuity team catalogs business processes, estimates the financial and operational impact of downtime for each over increasing durations, and identifies dependencies. This activity is the:
choices: Business impact analysis (BIA), which drives the RTO/RPO targets that recovery strategies must satisfy
ISC.explain: The BIA quantifies what downtime costs per process and surfaces dependencies; its outputs (criticality rankings, RTOs, RPOs) are the requirements that recovery-strategy selection must meet — which is why it comes first. (A) a pen test evaluates security defenses, not downtime impact. (C) disaster declaration is the moment a plan is INVOKED during an event. (D) a tabletop exercise TESTS a plan that already exists; the scenario describes building the analysis before the plan.

ISC.stem: The BIA sets a 2-hour RTO for a firm's customer-facing scheduling platform. Which recovery arrangement is the MINIMUM that can realistically meet this target?
choices: A cold site — empty space with power and HVAC where hardware would be delivered after a disaster
Relying on cyber insurance to reimburse downtime losses
A warm site with hardware installed but requiring roughly a day to load current data and configurations
A hot site (or cloud active/standby replication) kept current with near-real-time data, ready for rapid failover
ISC.explain: A 2-hour RTO demands infrastructure that is already running and current — a hot site or cloud failover with replicated data. (A) cold sites take days-to-weeks (procure, install, configure, restore). (B) encodes the risk-transfer misconception: insurance reimburses money; it restores nothing and satisfies no RTO. (C) a day-long activation misses a 2-hour target by an order of magnitude.

ISC.stem: A firm takes a full backup every Sunday night and incremental backups every other night. The server fails Thursday morning. How many backup sets must be restored, in order?
choices: Two — the Sunday full plus Wednesday's backup only
Seven — every backup from the past week regardless of type
Four — the Sunday full, then the Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday incrementals in sequence
ISC.explain: Incrementals capture only changes since the LAST backup of any kind, so restoration requires the last full plus every subsequent incremental in order: Sunday full + Mon + Tue + Wed = 4 sets. (A) encodes the differential misconception — only a DIFFERENTIAL (changes since last full) would allow full + most recent only. (B) an incremental alone holds just one day's changes. (C) overshoots; backups before the Sunday full are superseded.

ISC.stem: A CFO wants proof the firm can actually meet its declared 4-hour RTO for core systems, but the COO refuses any test that risks disrupting live production. Which testing approach BEST satisfies both constraints?
choices: A tabletop exercise where the team talks through the disaster scenario in a conference room
A checklist review confirming the plan document is up to date
A parallel/simulation test — actually failing over to and running recovery systems while production continues operating undisturbed
A full-interruption test that shuts down production to force real failover
ISC.explain: A parallel (simulation) test activates the recovery environment and processes test workloads alongside untouched production — the strongest evidence of real recovery capability, including timing, without production risk. (A) tabletop exercises validate decisions and roles but never touch technology, so they cannot prove a 4-hour technical RTO. (B) a document review proves even less — currency, not capability. (D) provides the best evidence but violates the COO's constraint by design; it is the option 'proof at any cost' would pick.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A cash-basis consultant's client hand-delivers a $12,000 check on December 29, Year 1. The consultant leaves it in a desk drawer and deposits it January 3, Year 2. In which year is the $12,000 gross income?
choices: Year 2, because a cash-basis taxpayer reports income when funds are deposited
Either year, at the taxpayer's election
Year 1 — the check was received without restriction, so the income was constructively (and actually) received in Year 1
Neither year until the client's invoice is formally closed
TCP.explain: A cash-basis taxpayer has income when cash or its equivalent is actually or constructively received — an unrestricted check in hand December 29 is Year 1 income; deliberately delaying deposit does not defer it. (A) encodes the deposit-date misconception; receipt, not deposit, controls. (B) encodes the misconception that timing is elective — the constructive receipt doctrine exists precisely to prevent that election. (D) invents an invoice-cycle rule with no basis in §451.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A MFJ couple has $28,000 of recurring itemized deductions each year (capped SALT plus mortgage interest) and normally gives $12,000 to charity annually. Assume a $32,600 MFJ standard deduction in both years. If they 'bunch' two years of giving ($24,000) into Year 1 and give $0 in Year 2, how much MORE do they deduct over the two years versus giving $12,000 each year?
choices: $0 — total gifts are identical, so total deductions are identical
TCP.explain: Unbunched: $28,000 + $12,000 = $40,000 itemized each year (exceeds $32,600), total $80,000. Bunched: Year 1 itemizes $28,000 + $24,000 = $52,000; Year 2 takes the $32,600 standard deduction; total $84,600. Extra = $84,600 − $80,000 = $4,600 — the standard deduction 'replaces' forgone itemizing in the off year. (B) encodes the misconception that equal cash outflow means equal deductions, ignoring the standard-deduction floor. (C) treats the shifted $12,000 gift as pure extra deduction. (D) is $52,000 − $32,600, comparing only Year 1's two options and ignoring Year 2 entirely.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: An investor in the 32% marginal bracket is choosing between a corporate bond yielding 5.0% and a municipal bond yielding 3.5%, equal risk. Which should she choose based on after-tax yield?
choices: The corporate bond, because 5.0% is greater than 3.5%
The corporate bond, because its after-tax yield is 3.60%
The municipal bond, because municipal bond interest is deductible
The municipal bond — the corporate bond's after-tax yield is 5.0% × (1 − 0.32) = 3.40%, below the tax-exempt 3.5%
TCP.explain: Compare after-tax yields: corporate 5.0% × 0.68 = 3.40% vs. municipal 3.5% tax-exempt. The muni wins by 10 basis points. (A) encodes the pre-tax comparison misconception — it ignores that corporate interest is fully taxable. (B) computes the after-tax yield with a 28% rate (5.0% × 0.72 = 3.60%) instead of the taxpayer's 32%. (C) reaches the right pick with wrong law: muni interest is EXCLUDED from income under §103, not 'deductible.'

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A MFJ couple has MAGI of $290,000, including $60,000 of net investment income. The NIIT threshold for MFJ is $250,000. Compute the net investment income tax.
TCP.explain: NIIT = 3.8% × the LESSER of net investment income ($60,000) or the MAGI excess over the threshold ($290,000 − $250,000 = $40,000). 3.8% × $40,000 = $1,520. (A) applies 3.8% to the full $60,000 NII, ignoring the lesser-of rule ($2,280). (C) applies 3.8% to a $90,000 excess computed with the $200,000 SINGLE-filer threshold ($3,420). (D) encodes the misconception that NIIT starts only at very high incomes such as $500,000.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: Under a divorce agreement executed in 2022, Dana pays her ex-spouse $30,000 per year of alimony. For 2026, how is it treated?
choices: Not deductible by Dana and not gross income to the recipient — the post-2018 rule applies
Deductible by Dana and gross income to the recipient
Gross income to the recipient, but not deductible by Dana
Deductible by Dana only as an itemized deduction
TCP.explain: For divorce or separation instruments executed after December 31, 2018, alimony is neither deductible by the payor nor includible by the recipient — and this treatment is permanent under the current baseline. (B) is the pre-2019 regime, which applies only to older, unmodified agreements. (C) creates asymmetric double taxation that exists under neither regime. (D) is doubly wrong — even under the old regime, alimony was an above-the-line deduction, never itemized.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a controller's weekend woodworking activity — properly classified as a hobby (no profit motive) — generates $8,000 of receipts and $5,000 of supplies expense. What is the effect on taxable income?
choices: Increase of $3,000 — hobby expenses offset hobby income
No effect — hobby income is not taxable
Increase of $8,000 — the receipts are gross income, and the expenses are nondeductible because miscellaneous itemized deductions are permanently terminated
Increase of $8,000 of income with a $5,000 miscellaneous itemized deduction subject to the 2% floor
TCP.explain: Hobby receipts are gross income under §61, but hobby expenses were deductible (if at all) only as miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deductions — a category PERMANENTLY terminated (P.L. 119-21 §70110). Net effect: +$8,000. (A) encodes the misconception that hobbies are taxed on net profit like a business. (B) confuses 'no profit motive' with 'no taxable income.' (D) applies the pre-termination 2% misc regime, which no longer exists in 2026.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 an executive exercises incentive stock options on 2,000 shares at a $10 strike price when the stock trades at $35, and holds the shares. What are the regular-tax and AMT consequences of the exercise?
choices: No regular-tax income; no AMT adjustment until the shares are sold
No regular-taxable income, but a $50,000 positive AMT adjustment — 2,000 × ($35 − $10) bargain element
$70,000 of ordinary income for both regular tax and AMT
$20,000 of ordinary income — 2,000 shares × the $10 strike price
TCP.explain: A qualifying ISO exercise produces no regular-tax income, but the bargain element — 2,000 × ($35 − $10) = $50,000 — is an AMT adjustment in the exercise year, the classic AMT trap that survives under the 2026 baseline. (A) encodes the misconception that AMT also waits for sale; the adjustment hits at EXERCISE when shares are held. (C) describes a NONQUALIFIED option, which generates ordinary income at exercise — ISOs do not. (D) multiplies shares by strike price, a number with no tax meaning here.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: An employer tells a cash-basis employee her $20,000 bonus check is ready for pickup December 30, Year 1. She waits and picks it up January 5, Year 2. Which statement is correct?
choices: Income can always be deferred by not collecting the check
The bonus is taxed when deposited, so it is Year 2 income
Asking payroll on December 31 to hold the available check shifts it to Year 2
The bonus is Year 1 income — it was made available without substantial restriction, so it was constructively received in Year 1
TCP.explain: Constructive receipt: income credited or set apart so the taxpayer may draw on it is taxed when made available, not when collected. Valid deferral requires arranging payment terms BEFORE the amount becomes available (e.g., an advance election under a deferred-comp plan). (A) and (B) restate the same deposit/collection misconception the doctrine forecloses. (C) fails because the request comes after availability — a taxpayer cannot 'turn his back' on income already available.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a MFJ couple pays $28,000 of state income tax and $18,000 of property tax. Their MAGI is well below the SALT phasedown threshold. What is their SALT itemized deduction?
choices: $46,000 — state and local taxes are fully deductible
TCP.explain: Total SALT paid is $46,000, but the 2026 cap is $40,400 (indexed from $40,000 in 2025) for taxpayers below the MAGI phasedown range — so they deduct $40,400. (B) ignores the cap entirely. (C) is the old TCJA-era $10,000 cap, which P.L. 119-21 §70120 replaced — $10,000 now survives only as the phasedown FLOOR for high earners. (D) is the MFS half-cap misapplied to a joint return.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a MFJ couple with MAGI of $600,000 pays $35,000 of state and local taxes. The 2026 SALT cap is $40,400, reduced by 30% of MAGI over $505,000, but not below a $10,000 floor. What is their SALT deduction?
choices: $10,000 — high-income taxpayers always drop to the floor
TCP.explain: Phasedown: excess MAGI = $600,000 − $505,000 = $95,000; reduction = 30% × $95,000 = $28,500; reduced cap = $40,400 − $28,500 = $11,900, which is above the $10,000 floor. Deduction = lesser of taxes paid ($35,000) or the reduced cap = $11,900. (A) jumps straight to the floor — the phasedown is gradual, and this couple's cap stops at $11,900. (B) ignores the cap/phasedown mechanism entirely. (D) applies the unreduced cap, ignoring the MAGI phasedown.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a site superintendent pays $4,200 of unreimbursed employee expenses (tools, mileage, union dues). How much is deductible on his federal return?
choices: The amount exceeding 2% of AGI, as a miscellaneous itemized deduction
$0 — miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deductions are permanently terminated under P.L. 119-21 §70110
$0 for 2026, but the deduction returns in 2027 when the suspension expires
TCP.explain: P.L. 119-21 §70110 permanently terminated the miscellaneous 2%-of-AGI itemized deduction category, so unreimbursed employee expenses yield $0 (the planning answer is an employer accountable plan). (A) is the pre-2018 regime. (C) invents above-the-line treatment that never applied to employee expenses generally (narrow exceptions like the educator deduction survive). (D) encodes the TCJA-sunset misconception — this is a permanent termination, not a suspension awaiting expiration.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A sole proprietor (not an SSTB, below all thresholds) has qualified business income of $180,000. Her taxable income before the QBI deduction is $160,000, which includes $10,000 of net capital gain. Compute the §199A deduction.
TCP.explain: The deduction is the LESSER of 20% × QBI (20% × $180,000 = $36,000) or 20% × (taxable income − net capital gain) = 20% × ($160,000 − $10,000) = $30,000. Answer: $30,000. (A) takes 20% of QBI and ignores the taxable-income limitation. (B) is 20% × $160,000, forgetting to remove net capital gain from the limit base. (C) is 20% × ($180,000 − $10,000), wrongly subtracting the capital gain from QBI instead of from taxable income.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A married taxpayer well above the §199A threshold owns a non-SSTB business with QBI of $400,000, W-2 wages of $120,000, and UBIA of qualified property of $600,000. Taxable income before QBI is $700,000 with no net capital gain. Compute the QBI deduction.
TCP.explain: Above the threshold the deduction is the lesser of 20% × QBI ($80,000) or the wage/UBIA limit — the GREATER of 50% × W-2 wages (50% × $120,000 = $60,000) or 25% × wages + 2.5% × UBIA ($30,000 + $15,000 = $45,000). Greater = $60,000; lesser of $80,000 vs. $60,000 = $60,000 (the 20%-of-taxable-income cap, $140,000, doesn't bind). (B) ignores the wage limitation. (C) uses the LESSER of the two wage tests instead of the greater. (D) is 20% of taxable income — the overall cap, not the deduction.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A consulting practice (a specified service trade or business) generates QBI of $300,000 and pays W-2 wages of $150,000. The owner's 2026 taxable income is $900,000 — far above the top of the SSTB phase-out range. What is her QBI deduction?
choices: $0 — SSTB income earns no QBI deduction once taxable income exceeds the full phase-out ceiling
TCP.explain: For an SSTB, once taxable income exceeds the top of the phase-out range the deduction is completely eliminated — no amount of W-2 wages rescues it. Answer: $0. (A) treats the business as a non-SSTB below the threshold. (B) applies the wage limit, which only matters for QUALIFIED businesses (or within the phase-out band) — above the ceiling, SSTB status zeroes everything first. (D) applies a fragment of the alternative wage/UBIA test to a situation where no deduction exists at all.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a taxpayer with AGI of $100,000 donates $30,000 cash to a public charity plus long-term appreciated stock worth $40,000 (basis $10,000). What is her current-year charitable deduction?
choices: $60,000 — $30,000 cash plus stock capped at 30% of AGI, with $10,000 carried forward up to five years
$30,000 — all gifts limited to 30% of AGI
TCP.explain: Cash to public charities is deductible up to 60% of AGI, so the $30,000 is fully allowed. Appreciated long-term-gain property is deducted at FMV but capped at 30% of AGI = $30,000; the excess $10,000 carries forward five years. Total current deduction $60,000. (A) ignores the 30% property ceiling. (C) wrongly deducts the stock at basis — FMV applies (that's the point of gifting appreciated stock: the gain is never taxed). (D) applies the 30% ceiling to the cash gift too.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In computing 2026 alternative minimum taxable income, which item does NOT get added back or otherwise adjusted?
choices: The bargain element of exercised-and-held incentive stock options
Tax-exempt interest on specified private-activity bonds
Charitable contributions of cash to public charities
TCP.explain: Charitable contributions are allowed for both regular tax and AMT — no addback. (A) the standard deduction is disallowed for AMT and effectively added back. (B) the ISO bargain element is a classic positive AMT adjustment at exercise. (C) specified private-activity-bond interest is a preference item includible in AMTI despite being tax-exempt for regular tax. The distractors are the three headline AMT triggers students most need to know still operate in 2026.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: Assume a $2,200-per-child child tax credit in 2026, phased out at $50 per $1,000 (or fraction) of MAGI above $400,000 MFJ. A MFJ couple with MAGI of $420,000 has three qualifying children under 17. Compute their credit.
TCP.explain: Tentative credit = 3 × $2,200 = $6,600. Phase-out = ($420,000 − $400,000) ÷ $1,000 = 20 increments × $50 = $1,000 reduction. Credit = $6,600 − $1,000 = $5,600. (B) forgets the phase-out entirely. (C) uses the outdated $2,000-per-child figure with no phase-out. (D) applies $100 per $1,000 instead of $50, doubling the reduction to $2,000.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A taxpayer in the 24% marginal bracket may claim either a $1,000 tax credit or a $1,000 deduction (not both). How much MORE tax does the credit save than the deduction?
TCP.explain: A credit reduces tax dollar-for-dollar ($1,000 saved); a deduction reduces taxable income, saving rate × amount = 24% × $1,000 = $240. Difference = $1,000 − $240 = $760. (A) encodes the misconception that credits and deductions are interchangeable. (B) is the value of the DEDUCTION, not the difference. (D) is the value of the CREDIT alone, ignoring that the deduction also saves something.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 an unmarried donor gives her son $50,000 cash. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What is her taxable gift?
choices: $0 — the lifetime exemption makes it nontaxable
TCP.explain: Taxable gift = $50,000 − $19,000 annual exclusion = $31,000. It consumes lifetime exemption (~$15M in 2026) so no tax is likely DUE, but the taxable-gift amount — which requires a gift-tax return and reduces the remaining exemption — is $31,000. (A) forgets the annual exclusion. (C) encodes the exclusion/exemption confusion: the exemption absorbs the tax, but the amount above the annual exclusion is still a taxable gift that must be reported. (D) subtracts a $38,000 split-gift exclusion unavailable to an unmarried donor.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a husband gives $38,000 from his separate account to each of his three children, and his wife consents to gift splitting on their gift-tax returns. The annual exclusion is $19,000. What are the couple's total taxable gifts?
choices: $0 — splitting treats each $38,000 gift as $19,000 from each spouse, fully covered by two annual exclusions per donee
TCP.explain: With gift splitting (§2513), each $38,000 gift is treated as made half by each spouse — $19,000 each — exactly matching each spouse's $19,000 annual exclusion per donee. 3 donees × $38,000 = $114,000, all excluded. (A) is the no-splitting answer: ($38,000 − $19,000) × 3 = $57,000 taxable to the husband. (B) applies no exclusions at all. (C) applies the exclusion to only one donee ($114,000 − $38,000) — the exclusion is per DONEE, not per donor.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A father gifts stock to his daughter when its FMV is $40,000; his basis is $60,000. She later sells it for $45,000. What gain or loss does she recognize?
TCP.explain: Dual-basis rule: for GAIN use the donor's $60,000 carryover basis ($45,000 sale → no gain); for LOSS use the $40,000 FMV at gift ($45,000 sale → no loss). Selling between the two bases produces neither. (A) uses the donor's basis to claim a loss — the loss basis is FMV, which blocks shifting the father's built-in loss. (B) uses the FMV loss basis to compute a GAIN, the mirror error. (D) simply takes the $60,000 − $40,000 built-in decline, which nobody recognizes.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: Same gift: donor's basis $60,000, FMV at gift $40,000. The daughter instead sells the stock for $35,000. What does she recognize?
choices: $5,000 loss — using the $40,000 FMV-at-gift loss basis
$0 — gifts of loss property never produce recognizable losses
TCP.explain: Selling below the FMV-at-gift figure triggers the loss basis: $35,000 − $40,000 = $5,000 loss. (B) uses the carryover basis for a loss sale — exactly what §1015 forbids, because it would transfer the donor's $20,000 built-in loss to the donee. (C) overreads the rule: losses ARE allowed, just measured from FMV at gift; only the pre-gift decline is disallowed. (D) has the wrong direction entirely — the sale price is below both bases.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: Which statement correctly describes the donee's holding period for gifted property?
choices: It always includes the donor's holding period
It always begins on the date of the gift
It includes the donor's holding period only if gift tax was paid
It includes (tacks) the donor's holding period when the carryover basis applies, but begins at the gift date when the FMV loss basis is used
TCP.explain: Tacking under §1223(2) follows the basis: when the donee's basis is determined by reference to the donor's (carryover/gain basis), the donor's holding period tacks; when the FMV-at-gift loss basis applies, the holding period starts fresh at the gift date. (A) ignores the loss-basis exception. (B) throws away tacking in the normal carryover case. (C) confuses tacking with the gift-tax basis ADJUSTMENT — paying gift tax can increase basis but is not what triggers tacking.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A decedent dying in 2026 leaves a taxable estate of $19,000,000, made no prior taxable gifts, and the basic exclusion is $15,000,000. Assuming a flat 40% rate on the excess, compute the estate tax.
TCP.explain: Tax = 40% × ($19,000,000 − $15,000,000) = 40% × $4,000,000 = $1,600,000 (the ~$15M P.L. 119-21 exemption absorbs the rest via the unified credit). (A) taxes the entire estate with no exemption. (C) encodes the misconception that the exemption is $30M for every estate — $30M applies only to a married COUPLE combining two exemptions (e.g., via portability). (D) is a decimal slip: 40% × $1.9M instead of $4.0M.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
