TCP.stem: A husband dies in 2026 having used $9,000,000 of his $15,000,000 exclusion; his executor timely elects portability. Ignoring future indexing, what total exclusion can his surviving wife's estate ultimately use?
choices: $15,000,000 — exclusions cannot be shared between spouses
$21,000,000 — her own $15,000,000 plus his $6,000,000 unused (DSUE) amount
TCP.explain: The DSUE amount is the deceased spouse's UNUSED exclusion: $15M − $9M = $6M. With a timely portability election, the survivor stacks it on her own $15M for a $21M total shield. (A) ignores portability, which has been available since 2011. (B) assumes both exclusions transfer in full even though $9M was already consumed. (D) adds the $9M USED portion instead of the $6M unused portion.

TCP.topic: Gift Now vs. Bequest — Basis Planning
TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A widow holds stock with basis $100,000, FMV $900,000. Option 1: gift it to her son now; he sells at $950,000. Option 2: he inherits it at her death (FMV then $900,000) and sells at $950,000. Assuming a combined 23.8% rate on long-term gains, how much capital-gains tax does inheriting SAVE versus the gift?
choices: $0 — the son's basis is the same either way
TCP.explain: Gift: carryover basis $100,000 → gain $850,000 → tax $202,300. Inheritance: §1014 step-up to $900,000 → gain $50,000 → tax $11,900. Savings = $202,300 − $11,900 = $190,400 (equivalently 23.8% × the $800,000 basis step-up). (B) is the entire gift-scenario tax, forgetting the heir still pays $11,900 on post-death appreciation. (C) is only the inheritance-scenario tax, not the savings. (D) encodes the misconception that death, like gifting, carries basis over — §1014 resets basis to date-of-death FMV.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A grandmother funds an irrevocable trust for her grandchildren and wants the contributions to qualify for the $19,000 annual exclusion. What is required?
choices: Nothing — all gifts in trust automatically qualify
Gifts in trust can never qualify for the annual exclusion
Filing a gift-tax return is sufficient to qualify the gifts
The beneficiaries must receive a present interest — typically a temporary right to withdraw contributions (a Crummey power)
TCP.explain: The annual exclusion applies only to PRESENT interests. A gift to a trust is normally a future interest — unless beneficiaries hold a Crummey withdrawal right, which converts each contribution into a present interest. (A) ignores the present-interest requirement entirely. (B) overcorrects; Crummey powers exist precisely to fix this. (C) confuses reporting with qualification — a Form 709 reports the gift but cannot transform a future interest into a present one.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a grandmother pays $80,000 of her grandson's tuition directly to the university and separately gives him $19,000 cash. What is her taxable gift?
choices: $0 — direct tuition payments are excluded without limit under §2503(e), and the cash is covered by the annual exclusion
TCP.explain: Tuition paid DIRECTLY to the educational institution is excluded from gift tax without dollar limit and without consuming the annual exclusion; the separate $19,000 cash gift fits exactly within the annual exclusion. Taxable gift: $0. (A) treats the tuition as a normal gift. (C) wastes the annual exclusion against the tuition ($80,000 − $19,000) and then taxes the cash. (D) excludes nothing. Key trap: the exclusion fails if the money is given TO the student to pay tuition — payment must go straight to the school.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: A profitable services business earns $150,000 per year. As a sole proprietorship, assume all of it faces 15.3% self-employment tax. As an S corporation paying its owner a reasonable $90,000 salary with the remaining $60,000 distributed, only the salary faces the 15.3% employment tax. Estimate the annual employment-tax savings from the S corporation structure.
choices: $0 — distributions are also subject to self-employment tax
TCP.explain: Savings = 15.3% × the $60,000 shifted from salary/SE income to distributions = $9,180. S corporation distributions to a shareholder-employee are not self-employment income (unlike a sole proprietor's entire net earnings), which is the core of this strategy — subject to the reasonable-compensation requirement. (A) states the sole-proprietorship rule as if it applied to S corp distributions. (B) is 15.3% × $150,000 — the total tax as a proprietor, not the SAVINGS. (D) is 15.3% × $90,000 — the tax still paid on the salary, not the savings.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: A C corporation earns $100,000, pays the 21% corporate tax, and distributes all remaining earnings as a qualified dividend taxed to the shareholder at 23.8% (20% + 3.8% NIIT). Compute the total combined tax.
TCP.explain: Corporate tax = 21% × $100,000 = $21,000. Dividend = $79,000; shareholder tax = 23.8% × $79,000 = $18,802. Combined = $21,000 + $18,802 = $39,802 (an effective 39.8% — the double-tax cost to weigh against pass-through treatment). (B) counts only the corporate layer. (C) applies both rates to the full $100,000 ($21,000 + $23,800), forgetting the dividend is the after-tax remainder. (D) counts only the shareholder layer.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: Which event would TERMINATE (or bar) a corporation's S election?
choices: Issuing voting and nonvoting common stock with identical distribution and liquidation rights
Admitting a resident-alien individual as a shareholder
Admitting a partnership as a shareholder
TCP.explain: S corporation shareholders must be individuals (plus certain estates, trusts, and exempt organizations) — a partnership shareholder terminates the election immediately. (A) 100 shareholders is exactly AT the limit, which permits up to 100. (B) differences in VOTING rights alone do not violate the one-class-of-stock rule as long as distribution/liquidation rights are identical. (C) the prohibition is on NONRESIDENT aliens; resident aliens are permissible shareholders.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: A partnership pays a partner a $96,000 guaranteed payment for services, determined without regard to partnership income. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is taxable to the partner only in years the partnership is profitable
It is ordinary income to the partner, subject to self-employment tax, and deductible by the partnership in computing ordinary business income
It is a qualified dividend taxed at capital-gain rates
It is exempt from self-employment tax because the partner is an owner, not an employee
TCP.explain: Guaranteed payments under §707(c) are compensation-like: ordinary income and SE income to the partner, and a deduction to the partnership regardless of profitability — the feature that distinguishes them from a distributive share. (A) describes a distributive share; guaranteed payments are payable and taxable even in loss years. (C) confuses partnerships with C corporations — partnerships pay no dividends. (D) is backwards: a general partner's service income, including guaranteed payments, is squarely SE income.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: A founder acquired qualified small business stock at original issue AFTER the July 2025 enactment of P.L. 119-21 and sells it after exactly 4 years, realizing a $2,000,000 gain (within the per-issuer cap). How much gain is taxable?
choices: $2,000,000 — no exclusion applies until the stock is held 5 years
TCP.explain: For post-enactment QSBS, P.L. 119-21 replaced the 5-year cliff with tiers: 50% exclusion after 3 years, 75% after 4, 100% after 5. At 4 years: 75% × $2,000,000 = $1,500,000 excluded; $500,000 taxable. (A) applies the 100% tier, which needs 5 years. (B) applies the 50% (3-year) tier. (D) is the OLD pre-enactment rule — an all-or-nothing 5-year requirement — which still governs older stock but not shares issued after enactment.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: Absent any election, how are (1) a two-member LLC and (2) a single-member LLC classified for federal income tax?
choices: (1) Partnership; (2) disregarded entity taxed directly to its owner
Both are automatically taxed as C corporations
Both must be taxed as C corporations unless they elect partnership status
TCP.explain: Default classifications under the check-the-box regulations: a domestic multi-member LLC is a partnership; a single-member LLC is disregarded (activity reported on the owner's return). Either may ELECT corporate treatment (and then S status if eligible). (B) and (D) reverse the regime — corporate treatment requires an affirmative election, never the default. (C) encodes the misconception that S status can arise by default; it always requires an eligible entity to elect corporate classification and file an S election.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: A single taxpayer sells her principal residence, which she owned and occupied for six years, realizing a $300,000 gain. She has not used the exclusion in the prior two years. What gain is taxable?
TCP.explain: A single filer meeting the 2-of-5-year ownership and use tests excludes up to $250,000; taxable gain = $300,000 − $250,000 = $50,000. (A) ignores §121 entirely. (B) applies the $500,000 MFJ exclusion to a single filer. (C) reports the EXCLUDED amount as the taxable amount — a swapped-labels error.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: A single taxpayer owned and used her home for only 12 months before selling at a $150,000 gain because her employer transferred her to a new city. Compute the taxable gain under the reduced (partial) exclusion.
choices: $150,000 — the two-year test was failed, so no exclusion applies
TCP.explain: A qualifying employment-related move allows a prorated CEILING: 12/24 × $250,000 = $125,000 maximum exclusion. Taxable gain = $150,000 − $125,000 = $25,000. (A) denies any relief — the reduced exclusion exists precisely for employment, health, and unforeseen-circumstance moves. (C) grants the full exclusion without the full two years. (D) prorates the GAIN (12/24 × $150,000 excluded) instead of prorating the $250,000 ceiling — the classic mechanical error.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: In 2026 an individual has an $8,000 net long-term capital loss and no capital gains. How is it used?
choices: Deduct all $8,000 against ordinary income this year
Deduct $3,000 this year; the remaining $5,000 is lost
Deduct $3,000 against ordinary income this year; carry the remaining $5,000 forward indefinitely
Deduct $0 — capital losses offset only capital gains
TCP.explain: Individuals net capital losses against gains, then deduct up to $3,000 (MFJ; $1,500 MFS) against ordinary income, carrying the excess forward indefinitely with its character preserved: $3,000 now, $5,000 carryover. (A) ignores the $3,000 annual limit. (B) forgets the indefinite carryforward. (D) states the CORPORATE rule — corporations get no ordinary-income offset (and only a 3-back/5-forward carry), individuals do.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: An investor exchanges business real estate (adjusted basis $280,000) for like-kind real estate worth $350,000 plus $50,000 cash. Compute the recognized gain.
choices: $50,000 — the lesser of realized gain ($120,000) or boot received ($50,000)
TCP.explain: Amount realized = $350,000 + $50,000 = $400,000; realized gain = $400,000 − $280,000 = $120,000. §1031 recognition = LESSER of realized gain or boot = $50,000. (B) recognizes the full realized gain, ignoring §1031 deferral. (C) ignores the boot — deferral is total only in a pure property-for-property swap. (D) reports the DEFERRED portion ($120,000 − $50,000) as recognized, inverting the split.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: Same exchange: basis given up $280,000; replacement property worth $350,000; $50,000 cash boot received; realized gain $120,000; recognized gain $50,000. What is the basis of the replacement property?
TCP.explain: Basis = adjusted basis given up + gain recognized − boot received = $280,000 + $50,000 − $50,000 = $280,000. Check: FMV of replacement ($350,000) − deferred gain ($70,000) = $280,000 ✓ — the deferred gain is embedded in a lower basis so it is taxed on the eventual sale. (A) uses cost/FMV basis, which would erase the deferral. (B) adds the recognized gain but forgets to subtract the boot. (C) subtracts the boot but forgets to add the recognized gain.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: A contractor sells equipment for $110,000. Original cost was $100,000 and $60,000 of depreciation was taken (adjusted basis $40,000). Characterize the $70,000 gain.
choices: $70,000 of §1231 gain eligible for long-term capital-gain rates
$60,000 of ordinary income (§1245 recapture) and $10,000 of §1231 gain
$10,000 of ordinary income and $60,000 of §1231 gain
TCP.explain: Gain = $110,000 − $40,000 = $70,000. §1245 recaptures as ordinary income the LESSER of depreciation taken ($60,000) or gain ($70,000) → $60,000 ordinary; the $10,000 excess (sale price over original cost) is §1231 gain. (A) ignores recapture entirely. (C) recaptures more than the depreciation taken — the excess over original cost was never depreciation. (D) inverts the two components.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: An investor sells a commercial building held for years, recognizing a $150,000 gain. Straight-line depreciation of $200,000 was taken. How much is 'unrecaptured §1250 gain' taxed at the maximum 25% rate?
choices: $0 — straight-line depreciation on realty never affects the tax rate
$150,000 — the lesser of depreciation taken or the recognized gain
TCP.explain: Unrecaptured §1250 gain = the LESSER of straight-line depreciation taken ($200,000) or the recognized gain ($150,000) = $150,000, taxed at a maximum 25% rather than the usual LTCG rates. (A) uses ALL depreciation taken even though it exceeds the gain — the amount can never exceed gain recognized. (B) confuses the 25%-rate rule with §1250 ORDINARY recapture (which is indeed $0 for straight-line) — the 25% bucket still applies. (D) is the meaningless difference $200,000 − $150,000.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: A taxpayer sells stock (basis $100,000) to her brother for $80,000, and the $20,000 loss is disallowed under §267. The brother later sells the stock to an unrelated buyer for $95,000. What does the brother recognize?
choices: $0 — his $15,000 realized gain is fully offset by the previously disallowed loss
$15,000 gain to the brother, and the sister may amend her return to deduct her $20,000 loss
TCP.explain: The related buyer's gain is reduced (but not below zero) by the seller's disallowed loss: realized gain $95,000 − $80,000 = $15,000, offset by up to $20,000 of disallowed loss → $0 recognized. The remaining $5,000 of disallowed loss simply disappears. (B) ignores the offset rule. (C) uses the full $20,000 against the $15,000 gain to create a loss — the offset cannot go below zero. (D) lets the loss revert to the original seller, which §267 never allows.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: Land with a basis of $300,000 is sold for $500,000, payable $100,000 per year for five years (ignore interest). Under the installment method, how much gain is recognized in Year 1?
TCP.explain: Gross profit = $200,000; gross profit percentage = $200,000 ÷ $500,000 = 40%. Year 1 gain = 40% × $100,000 collected = $40,000. (A) treats all cash received as gain, ignoring basis recovery. (B) recognizes the entire gain in the year of sale — that happens only if the taxpayer ELECTS OUT of installment reporting. (C) applies the basis-recovery percentage (60%) instead of the gross-profit percentage.

TCP.blueprintArea: Property Transactions (Disposition of Assets)
TCP.stem: An investor sells 100 shares at a $4,000 loss on December 20 and repurchases 100 identical shares for $12,000 on January 8 — 19 days later. What is the result?
choices: The $4,000 loss is deductible, and the new shares take a $12,000 basis
The loss is disallowed under the wash-sale rule, and the new shares take a $16,000 basis ($12,000 cost + $4,000 disallowed loss)
The loss is disallowed permanently, and the new shares take a $12,000 basis
Only $3,000 of the loss is deductible this year
TCP.explain: Repurchasing substantially identical securities within 30 days before or after a loss sale triggers §1091: the loss is disallowed but PRESERVED by adding it to the replacement shares' basis ($16,000), and the holding period tacks. (A) ignores the wash-sale window (19 days < 30). (C) treats the disallowance as permanent — the basis addback defers, not destroys, the loss. (D) confuses the wash-sale rule with the $3,000 annual capital-loss limit, which never comes into play because no loss is currently allowed.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Compliance
TCP.stem: An S corporation shareholder begins the year with $30,000 stock basis. During the year her K-1 shows: ordinary income $20,000, tax-exempt interest $5,000, a $40,000 cash distribution, and a $20,000 ordinary loss. Applying the basis-ordering rules (income first, then distributions, then losses), how much loss may she deduct this year?
TCP.explain: Ordering: basis $30,000 + $20,000 income + $5,000 tax-exempt = $55,000; distribution $40,000 (nontaxable — within basis) reduces basis to $15,000; the $20,000 loss is then limited to the $15,000 remaining basis, with $5,000 suspended until basis is restored. (A) ignores the basis limitation. (B) assumes the distribution wipes out all loss capacity. (D) forgets that tax-exempt income ALSO increases basis ($30,000 + $20,000 − $40,000 = $10,000) — omitting the $5,000 exempt-interest step.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Compliance
TCP.stem: A partner contributes property with an adjusted basis of $50,000 (FMV $80,000) subject to a $20,000 recourse liability the partnership assumes. Her share of partnership liabilities is 25%. Compute her initial outside basis.
TCP.explain: Outside basis = basis of property contributed $50,000 − liability shifted to OTHER partners (75% × $20,000 = $15,000 deemed cash distribution) = $35,000. Equivalently: $50,000 − $20,000 relief + $5,000 retained share. (B) ignores the liability shift entirely. (C) subtracts the full $20,000 relief but forgets she keeps her own 25% share ($5,000) as a deemed contribution. (D) uses FMV — contributions to partnerships take carryover basis under §722, not FMV.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Compliance
TCP.stem: A partner with an outside basis of $25,000 receives a $40,000 current (non-liquidating) cash distribution. What does she recognize?
choices: $15,000 of capital gain — cash distributed in excess of outside basis
TCP.explain: Cash distributions reduce outside basis first; only the excess over basis is taxable: $40,000 − $25,000 = $15,000, treated as gain from the sale of the partnership interest — capital gain. (A) states the general nonrecognition rule but ignores its limit at zero basis. (B) taxes the entire distribution, ignoring basis recovery. (C) has the right amount but the wrong character — the excess is capital, not ordinary (absent §751 hot-asset issues).

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Compliance
TCP.stem: A C corporation elects S status on January 1, 2026, holding land with a $200,000 built-in gain at conversion. The S corporation sells the land in 2027 — within the 5-year recognition period. What entity-level tax results (21% corporate rate)?
choices: $0 — S corporations never pay entity-level federal income tax
$42,000 of built-in gains tax at the corporate level, and the gain (less the tax) also passes through to shareholders
$47,600 — the gain is taxed at the 23.8% shareholder capital-gains rate
$84,000 — the gain is taxed at both the corporate and shareholder level at 21% each
TCP.explain: §1374 imposes a corporate-level tax on net recognized built-in gain sold within 5 years of conversion: 21% × $200,000 = $42,000; the gain also flows through to shareholders (reduced by the tax paid). Waiting out the 5-year period would have avoided it. (A) overstates the pass-through rule — BIG tax, excess net passive income tax, and LIFO recapture are entity-level exceptions. (C) applies the shareholder rate at the entity level. (D) invents a double 21% — the corporate BIG tax plus SHAREHOLDER-level pass-through tax is the real structure, not two corporate taxes.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: In 2026 a C corporation with taxable income (before the charitable deduction) of $1,000,000 contributes $85,000 cash to public charities. Under P.L. 119-21 §70426, contributions are deductible only to the extent they EXCEED 1% of taxable income, up to the 10% ceiling. Compute the deduction.
TCP.explain: Floor = 1% × $1,000,000 = $10,000; ceiling = 10% × $1,000,000 = $100,000. Deduction = $85,000 − $10,000 floor = $75,000 (well under the ceiling). Amounts disallowed by the ceiling carry forward five years. (A) applies the pre-2026 rule with no 1% floor. (B) deducts the ceiling rather than the contribution actually made. (D) deducts the floor itself — the floor is the DISALLOWED band, not the deduction.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: The sole shareholder-employee of a profitable S corporation works full-time managing the business but takes no salary, withdrawing $180,000 as distributions to avoid payroll taxes. The PRIMARY tax risk is:
choices: The IRS recharacterizes distributions as wages, assessing employment taxes, penalties, and interest on a reasonable-compensation amount
None — S corporation distributions are always tax-free to shareholders
The distributions become qualified dividends taxed at 15%
The S election terminates automatically after one year of zero salary
TCP.explain: Rev. Rul. 74-44 and abundant case law let the IRS recharacterize distributions as reasonable compensation for services actually rendered, retroactively imposing FICA/FUTA, penalties, and interest. The savings strategy works only with a defensible salary. (B) confuses basis-covered distributions being income-tax-free with immunity from wage recharacterization. (C) imports C corporation dividend treatment into an S corporation. (D) invents a termination trigger — compensation practices, however aggressive, do not terminate an S election.

TCP.topic: Sale of Partnership Interest — Hot Assets
TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Planning
TCP.stem: A partner sells his partnership interest for a total gain of $100,000. His share of the partnership's unrealized receivables (a §751 'hot asset') is $30,000. How is the gain characterized?
choices: $100,000 capital gain — a partnership interest is a capital asset
TCP.explain: §751 overrides the general capital treatment: the portion of the gain attributable to unrealized receivables and inventory ($30,000) is ordinary income; the remaining $70,000 is capital gain. This prevents converting ordinary income (like uncollected fees) into capital gain via a sale of the interest. (A) applies the entity theory without the §751 carve-out. (B) overcorrects, treating everything as ordinary. (C) inverts the two components.

TCP.blueprintArea: Entity Tax Compliance
TCP.stem: A corporation has taxable income of $100,000 in 2026 (before any NOL deduction) and a $150,000 NOL carryforward that arose in 2023. How much NOL may it deduct in 2026?
choices: $80,000 — post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income; the remaining $70,000 carries forward indefinitely
$0 — NOLs may only be carried back
TCP.explain: Post-2017 NOLs carry forward indefinitely (no general carryback) but may offset only 80% of taxable income: 80% × $100,000 = $80,000 deducted, leaving $20,000 taxable and a $70,000 carryforward. (A) applies the pre-2018 100% offset rule. (C) deducts beyond taxable income — NOLs cannot create negative income or refunds. (D) reverses the rule: carrybacks are what post-2017 law generally ELIMINATED.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A 28-year-old associate in the 12% bracket expects to be in a much higher bracket in retirement. For new retirement contributions, the tax-optimal choice is generally:
choices: A traditional (pre-tax) account, because deferral always wins
Neither — a taxable brokerage account beats both
A Roth account — pay tax now at 12% and withdraw tax-free later at the higher expected rate
A traditional account, because Roth contributions are deductible
TCP.explain: The Roth-vs-traditional decision turns on current versus expected future marginal rates: pay 12% now (Roth) rather than deduct at 12% and later withdraw at a higher rate (traditional). (A) encodes the 'deferral always wins' misconception — deferral loses when the future rate is higher. (B) forfeits tax-advantaged growth entirely. (D) contains a factual error: Roth contributions are NEVER deductible; that is the traditional side's feature.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A 50-year-old converts $50,000 from a traditional IRA (all pre-tax) to a Roth IRA in a year when her marginal rate is 22%, paying the tax from outside funds. What is the immediate federal income-tax cost, and does the 10% early-distribution penalty apply?
choices: $11,000 of tax; no 10% penalty — a proper conversion is not a penalized early distribution
TCP.explain: A conversion is taxable as ordinary income: 22% × $50,000 = $11,000, but it is exempt from the §72(t) 10% penalty (though converted amounts have their own 5-year clock for penalty-free withdrawal). Paying the tax with outside funds keeps the full $50,000 growing tax-free. (B) confuses conversions with trustee-to-trustee ROLLOVERS between like accounts. (C) wrongly adds the early-distribution penalty to a conversion. (D) applies the penalty INSTEAD of the income tax — backwards on both counts.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A 45-year-old in the 24% bracket withdraws $20,000 from his traditional IRA (all pre-tax) to buy a boat — no exception applies. Compute the total federal cost of the withdrawal.
choices: $0 — IRA withdrawals are a tax-free return of the owner's own money
$6,800 — $4,800 income tax plus a $2,000 early-distribution penalty
TCP.explain: The distribution is ordinary income (24% × $20,000 = $4,800) PLUS the §72(t) 10% additional tax ($2,000) because he is under 59½ with no exception (no first home, education, disability, etc.): total $6,800 — a 34% haircut that makes early withdrawals a last resort. (A) forgets the penalty. (B) counts only the penalty. (C) confuses pre-tax traditional IRA dollars with Roth basis — nothing here was previously taxed.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: Which statement correctly describes the federal tax treatment of a §529 education savings plan?
choices: Contributions are deductible on the federal return
Earnings grow tax-deferred and are tax-FREE when withdrawn for qualified education expenses
Earnings are always taxable when withdrawn, regardless of use
Only tuition at in-state public universities qualifies
TCP.explain: The federal benefit is on the back end: no deduction going in, but earnings escape tax entirely when distributions pay qualified education expenses. Contributions are also completed gifts eligible for the annual exclusion (with a 5-year front-loading election). (A) confuses the occasional STATE deduction with federal law — there is no federal deduction. (C) describes nonqualified withdrawals only (earnings portion taxed plus 10% penalty). (D) invents a residency/institution restriction — eligible institutions nationwide (and certain K-12 and apprenticeship costs) qualify.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A taxpayer owing $10,000 files his return and pays in full exactly 3 months after the (unextended) due date. The failure-to-file penalty is 5% per month (reduced by the concurrent 0.5% failure-to-pay penalty), each capped at 25%. Compute the total combined penalty.
TCP.explain: When both penalties run concurrently, the combined charge is 5% per month (4.5% FTF + 0.5% FTP): 5% × 3 × $10,000 = $1,500. The lesson: FILE on time even if you cannot pay — filing alone drops the monthly rate from 5% to 0.5%. (A) is the FTP-only amount ($10,000 × 0.5% × 3), as if the return had been timely filed. (B) stacks the full 5% FTF on top of the 0.5% FTP without the offset (5.5% × 3). (D) jumps straight to the 25% maximum, which takes 5 months to reach.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: An individual's correct tax was $60,000 but she reported $48,000 — a $12,000 understatement with no disclosure and no substantial authority. The substantial-understatement threshold is the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000. Compute the accuracy-related penalty.
choices: $2,400 — the understatement exceeds $6,000, so the 20% penalty applies to the $12,000
$0 — the understatement is under 25% of gross income
TCP.explain: Threshold = greater of 10% × $60,000 = $6,000 or $5,000 → $6,000. The $12,000 understatement exceeds it, so the §6662 20% penalty applies: 20% × $12,000 = $2,400. Defenses — substantial authority or reasonable basis plus disclosure — are absent. (B) imports the 25%-omission test from the six-year STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS rule, a different provision. (C) applies 20% to the $48,000 reported tax instead of the understatement. (D) confuses the penalty with the understatement itself (a 100% rate).

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A taxpayer timely filed a non-fraudulent return reporting $200,000 of gross income but omitted an additional $60,000 of gross income. How long does the IRS have to assess additional tax?
choices: 3 years from filing — the standard assessment period
Unlimited — any omission leaves the year open forever
6 years from filing — the omission ($60,000) exceeds 25% of the gross income stated on the return ($50,000)
TCP.explain: Omitting more than 25% of reported gross income extends the assessment statute to 6 years: $60,000 > 25% × $200,000 = $50,000, so 6 years applies. (A) is the default period, displaced by the substantial omission. (B) describes FRAUD or failure to file, where the period never closes — an honest omission is not fraud. (C) confuses the ASSESSMENT statute with the 10-year COLLECTION statute that starts after assessment.

TCP.blueprintArea: Tax Compliance and Planning for Individuals and Personal Financial Planning
TCP.stem: A taxpayer's prior-year AGI was $310,000 and prior-year tax was $40,000. This year's income will be dramatically higher and hard to estimate. To be penalty-proof using the prior-year safe harbor, his withholding plus timely estimates must total at least:
choices: $44,000 — 110% of prior-year tax, because prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000
TCP.explain: Individuals avoid the §6654 penalty by paying the lesser of 90% of the current-year tax or 100% of prior-year tax — bumped to 110% of prior-year tax when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000. Since current-year tax is high and uncertain, the reliable target is 110% × $40,000 = $44,000. (A) uses the 100% safe harbor available only to lower-AGI taxpayers. (C) applies 90% to the PRIOR year's tax — the 90% test applies to the CURRENT year's tax. (D) invents a 125% requirement that does not exist.
